newsitem.title: CANADA: Middle East oil expert sees mid-1997 price crash.
newsitem.headline: Middle East oil expert sees mid-1997 price crash.

text.p: World oil prices could crash to as low as US$8 per barrel next year if Saudi Arabia and its Gulf OPEC allies bring on stream an estimated three million barrels per day in efforts to curb output from other producing nations, a top Middle East oil expert said on Monday.

Joseph Story, president of Virginia-based Gulf Consulting Services and a former policy adviser to Saudi Aramco, said he expected prices to fall to between US$8 and US$12 per barrel "only for a matter of months -- long enough to scare everything."

Saudi Arabia and allies Kuwait and United Arab Emirates, the only OPEC nations with large amounts of shut-in production, have grown weary of quota cheating among other OPEC producers and strong production growth from non-OPEC nations, Story told reporters after a speech to an oil industry conference.
"What I've heard is the Saudis hope that by getting OPEC back together, maybe a few non-OPEC countries like Yemen and Oman might cut back," he said.
He said that as soon as factors today making the oil market buoyant, such as low inventories and uncertainty surrounding Iraq exports, are gone, the new production would be gradually brought on.
Current Saudi Arabian output is about 8.1 million barrels per day. Story said it could add another two million barrels per day and Kuwait and UAE could each add 500,000 barrels per day.
He said, however, the three nations would likely open the taps for only a few months because of needs to increase oil revenues for their own battered economies.

"The Saudis are only going to do it until they see the reaction. They don't want to push it down to US$5 a barrel, but they want to make an impression," he said, adding the moves would likely be made in the middle of 1997.
Asked how confident he was in his projection, Story said: "I don't know of anybody who either has the access or knows as much about Saudi Arabia as I do."

Sean O'Dell, chief economist for the International Energy Agency, said the scenario was possible, although not the best strategy for Saudi Arabia. "I think it's entirely possible in the short run," O'Dell said.

He said a return to the world market of Iraqi crude, a warm winter in consuming nations and a recession in one of the world's fast-developing regions were possible other factors that would lead to steep drop in oil prices.
But if Saudi Arabia proceeds with pushing up output, the may backfire because its economy would be taking in possibly the same revenue from the production of more oil at lower prices, O'Dell said.
He said that OPEC's best stragy would be to attempt to stave off large price spikes and collapses, which would cement customer confdience in the group's supply.
The IEA projects average prices will remain relatively flat through the rest of the decade, he said. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
